briefs.title: When Building Is Cheap, Judgment Is the Product
briefs.body:
Two conversations on Lenny's Podcast this week, one with Google's head of frontier-model product and one with the 22-year-old behind Wispr Flow's growth engine, look unrelated. One is about shaping models nobody fully controls; the other is about marketing a voice-dictation app. Read together, they make the same argument: when building and shipping get cheap, the scarce thing is judgment about what is real, and the best operators protect that judgment with unglamorous human habits.

Start with Tulsee Doshi, who runs product for Gemini, the Gen Media models (Nano Banana, Lyria), the open Gemma family and Google's audio models. Her first claim is that model product management breaks the usual contract. In a conventional product you set goals and the team delivers them. A model, she says, is "like Snape's potions class": you choose the ingredients carefully, but you must expect some magic you didn't plan. The PM's job is therefore twofold. Shape what goes in, then study what comes out, find where the model unexpectedly shines, and build the product around that. She wants PMs who "understand the vibes" of models, who play with them daily and stress-test them on things they care about.

That shapes her build philosophy, the "60/20/20 rule." Classic startup advice says to ship an MVP that works. Doshi's version is that 60% of what you build should work today, 20% should work well enough to hint at where the models are going, and the last 20% is a bet on capabilities you've only glimpsed. You ship something real now, and the product can grow as the models do. It is more practical than the common advice to "build three months ahead," because it doesn't ask you to bet everything on a forecast.

On the PM role itself she is blunt about the slogans. "Prototype is the new PRD," "evals are the new PRD," "data is the new PRD": what these really show, she argues, is that the work has moved from documents to artifacts you can interact with. AI has made prototyping and data analysis nearly free for PMs. So what is left? Taste, meaning the ability to separate signal from noise and find the insight that unlocks an experience, and the ability to turn chaos into order. When everyone can build fast, speed alone produces chaos, and someone has to bring clarity and consensus. That is her case for why PMs are "suddenly valuable again." She also offers a useful heuristic for delegating to AI: if you have to do something twice, ask whether you need to do it yourself. Writing a strategy twice, yes. Most other things, probably not.

Now Hector Serrano. He joined Wispr Flow at 19 as a UGC creator, asked for equity on day two, and now runs its paid UGC program while the company's revenue has reportedly grown 30x in a year. His starting point echoes Doshi's: the product comes first. There is no growth hack, he says, only a product good enough to grow on its own, to which you then add levers. If it isn't growing organically, go back and rethink positioning rather than forcing it.

From there his advice is tactical, and counterintuitive in places. Turn on paid early, with an e-commerce mindset, because paid tells you fast whether your messaging converts cold traffic. Wispr's first attempt, organic UGC paid by CPM, produced around 500 million views in two and a half months but not many conversions; it chased vanity metrics. The paid program that followed works the other way: recruit talented, small-following creators, leave them free to experiment, and do not cap their earnings. Some now make around $13,000 a month with only a thousand or two followers of their own. His argument is that audiences distrust famous faces who have sold products for ten years, and an unknown creator's partnership ad feels more genuine.

His hiring advice is just as deliberately low-tech. Don't post high-salary listings on LinkedIn; you attract the wrong people. Look for hungry people who have grown an account, even to 10,000 followers, and who understand trends, editing and consistency. Young people living in the feeds understand the channels better than a 35-year-old founder does, he argues, and a flat team of roughly 15 marketers, with no middle management, lets them act on that.

The sharpest overlap is about AI. Doshi says AI makes building trivial and so makes judgment the differentiator. Serrano says "the best marketers are allergic to AI" for final creative output. Slop ads are noise, quality over quantity cuts through, and even the most automation-heavy person he knows keeps a human on the last 10%, because a brand cannot afford a visible mistake. Both are describing the same discipline: let machines expand what you can produce, but keep a person accountable for what actually ships.

One more short but telling voice supports this. A snippet on design partners warns that they usually "buy into your vision," give lots of feedback and never buy. People with a real, urgent problem want it solved, not to co-design your product. Enthusiastic input is not demand. Whether you're evaluating model behavior, a creator's video or a design partner's praise, the lesson is to look for the signal that costs the other side something: usage, conversions, money.

The takeaway for product leaders is uncomfortable but simple. Tools have made the cheap parts of the job cheaper. What remains is deciding what's worth building, noticing when a result is surprising rather than merely plausible, hiring for hunger over credentials, and refusing to confuse feedback and views with traction.

briefs.title: The Last Constraint on AI Is a Vote
briefs.body:
The AI industry has spent three years explaining its bottlenecks in engineering terms: first compute, then memory, then power. This week three very different voices pointed at the same thing from three angles, and it was not an engineering problem.

Ben Thompson of Stratechery opened with the election. Democrats took both chambers of Congress, but what Thompson noticed, watching a season of baseball ads in Wisconsin, was that data centers were the most common campaign topic, and both parties ran against them. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa won the governorship pledging a moratorium on construction, even though incumbent Greg Abbott had already frozen new data-center permits in September. Nearly every local ballot measure against data centers has won, with North Dakota the lone exception. His thesis: the constraint on AI's spread has moved again. Compute ramped, memory will ramp, power will be fixed. The final constraint is political, and it interferes with solving the other three.

His explanation is sharp. Globalization hit Rust Belt towns without asking them. Data centers require permission, so people who had no say in the last disruption finally have one, and the industry's own pitch, that AI replaces labor, gives them a reason to use it. Thompson then runs ten scenarios for a world with a permanently impaired ability to build. Neoclouds suffer because they now need permits as well as capital. Hyperscalers win share, and political cover to moderate spending. Nvidia loses volume near term but gains pricing power, since tokens per megawatt matters more when power is scarce. China gains, because it has electricity and can brute-force its way past weaker chips. Frontier labs benefit because the public is effectively pacing a race that was bankrupting them. Startups suffer, and Apple gains.

Aswath Damodaran, the NYU valuation professor, arrives at the same place from the money side. Asked about a $20 trillion addressable market, his answer is "tell me why, tell me how, tell me where." Over $2 trillion is already in the ground, which he notes exceeds the railroads and the dot-com build-out. His worry is not Meta or Alphabet, whose advertising businesses can absorb a write-down. It is the CoreWeaves, which have no cash cow and so fund data centers with debt and private credit. When the correction comes, he argues, those facilities default, and debt default becomes everyone's pain, as it did in 2008, when the losses reached depositors and the real economy rather than staying with equity holders. He says that correction "has to come sometime."

Damodaran adds two cautions that cut against easy bearishness. First, selling everything to sit in cash at four or five percent has a hidden cost: the people who dodged 2008 often ended up poorer than those who rode it out, because getting back in is hard. Second, if you avoid the AI names entirely you can escape much of the damage, as non-dot-com holders did in 2001, but this time it is harder because AI touches everything. He also says to watch what markets price rather than what experts say, noting that markets beat experts in 2020.

Matt Wolfe's look at Anthropic's new Fable 5.2 is the counterpoint, and it is useful precisely because it shows how much capability is still arriving. The benchmarks show real but not monumental gains: agentic scientific research rose from 58.7 to 74.6 percent, while agentic coding moved from 45.5 to 49.1. Anthropic's own demos include a prototype operating system built by over 1,000 sub-agents over eight days. But Wolfe stresses the economics. At $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, it costs double Opus 5.5, and the average task on Artificial Analysis cost $26.54 at max reasoning. More striking, thinking longer actually scored worse than "extra high" on one coding benchmark while costing more. His own game-building test took 16 minutes and worked on the first try, yet his recommendation was that Opus 5.5 remains the daily driver for most people.

Read together, these are one story. Models are getting smarter at a rate that justifies enormous spending, but each step costs more, the money is increasingly borrowed, and the physical sites to spend it on now require a public that is saying no. Thompson thinks scarcity may last far longer than commodity-minded forecasts assumed. Damodaran thinks the financing structure turns any stumble into a credit event. Wolfe's numbers show why labs and buyers will care about efficiency over raw power.

The practical takeaway is that the winners of this phase are probably not whoever has the best model, but whoever has permitted capacity, cheap tokens per watt, and a balance sheet that doesn't depend on refinancing. AI wasn't formally on the ballot, as Thompson put it, but it will be from now on.

briefs.title: Building the Rails Inside Someone Else's Rules
briefs.body:
Three conversations this week, about India's payments network, India's oldest IT services giant, and America's leading robotaxi company, tell the same story. Infrastructure businesses are not won by the best technology. They are won by whoever learns to operate inside regulators, incumbents and public suspicion.

Start with UPI. On Nikhil Kamath's show, NPCI's Sohini, Razorpay co-founder Harshil Mathur and PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam spent hours explaining something they agree nobody has properly written down: how a hundred-rupee transfer actually moves. The app sends a message through a sponsor bank to NPCI, which resolves the virtual payment address to a bank account, confirms with the recipient's bank, checks funds at the sender's bank, and nets settlements out at the end of the cycle. The app never touches the money. The point they kept returning to was how much hidden complexity sits under something that feels like a sound. Mathur's origin story makes the same case from the other side: he and his co-founder built a crowdfunding side project, found accepting payments nearly impossible through banks with 1990s-era interfaces, and discovered that everyone around them just took cash on delivery.

The economics are the uncomfortable part, and the title question, who pays for free UPI, is left partly open. Nigam described how PhonePe had around 30 million QR codes on the person-to-person rail before the government announced zero merchant fees, and how the regulator eventually agreed to a formal P2PM category so small shops would not be charged up to one lakh rupees. India, he noted, is the only market with such a code. Both founders also pushed back on regulatory paternalism, a "very avuncular" instinct that assumes users must be protected from products. Mathur's Flipkart sale story, in which millions of card attempts failed, banks' core systems went down, and tens of thousands of televisions were sold with no payment record, shows what scaling on someone else's rails looks like. They closed by expecting real-time networks to interconnect faster than central bank digital currencies ever will.

The Ken's Intermission episode on TCS is the older version of this lesson. TCS began in 1968 as a division of Tata Sons running data processing on leased mainframes, and its defining move was flexibility. Its partnership with Burroughs turned into a crisis when Tata Sons wanted to fold TCS into a joint venture that would control all Burroughs work. The Indian government, in the licence-raj era, told the Tatas to keep the crown jewel independent, and that forced TCS to find its own customers. It also took the government to court after computers were classified alongside toasters and electric razors, taxed above 100 percent, and won a refund in 1980. Later, Y2K opened doors to clients who would never have outsourced to an unknown Indian firm. The episode's useful number is the 2007 comparison: Accenture earned 2.5 times TCS's revenue per employee, but the operating profit per employee was comparable.

Then there is Waymo. Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana told Bloomberg's Emily Chang that the company counts a Waymo roughly every minute in San Francisco. She cites an insurance-institute study showing 68 percent fewer crashes than human drivers, yet a 2026 Pew poll shows 71 percent of adults uncomfortable in a driverless car. The company is dealing with school-bus signals, flooded streets, a Senate hearing where it emerged that remote assistants work from the Philippines, and a senator's complaint about Zeekr-built vehicles. Mawakana's answer on a fatal accident is notable for its humility: there will be one, and it will be a hard day. Her reframing is that society already accepts many deaths from human drivers. On price, rides average about $9.58 per mile versus $6.88 for Uber and $6.41 for Lyft, and she says price is not the first priority.

What connects the three is that the technology was never the scarce thing. NPCI and the private apps had to negotiate who bears the cost of free payments. TCS survived licensing, joint-venture politics and tariff categories. Waymo has to convince a nervous public, city officials and senators while its mistakes go viral. Each firm describes its edge as adaptability, and the TCS episode even quotes Bruce Lee on being like water.

For builders, the lesson is that the product is only half the work. The moat is the relationship with the institution that can switch you off.

briefs.title: When the Story Changes, Trust the Rules
briefs.body:
Every market narrative eventually asks you to believe a story. Three Indian investing voices this week, each from a different angle, argue that the way to survive is to have a process that doesn't care what the story is.

Manish Dhawan of Mystic Wealth is the clearest on method. He started in 2007, built a strategy around demergers and spin-offs, left a corporate job in 2011 with about 22 lakh rupees plus money from family and friends, and says early on he was lucky, since at times 30 percent of net worth sat in one stock. His realization is that everything in markets is a story someone is selling, and that once your buying and selling are driven by a process, you stop listening to television. His momentum system is simple to state. Take the top 750 stocks, rank them by speed of price rise, penalize volatility, and also rank by distance from the 52-week high. Buy the top 20 at equal weight, so 4 percent each if 80 percent invested. Rebalance monthly, keep a stock until it falls below rank 50, and replace it with a newcomer. A hundred-year backtest, he says, shows better returns than the Nifty or Nifty 500.

He is candid about the cost. Plain momentum can draw down 30 to 35 percent, and a typical mutual fund fell 70 percent in 2008. His arithmetic on recovery is why that matters: a 50 percent loss needs a 100 percent gain, and a 70 percent loss needs 300 percent. Roughly 60 percent of his picks lose money, so "we are worse than a coin toss," but the winners are large. Because his partner runs a value strategy and he runs momentum, he combines the two, inspired by Ray Dalio's advice on uncorrelated strategies, though he concedes both remain tied to the market. He also names today's story: AI, then data centers, and now, as AI sours, IT stocks as an "anti-AI" trade.

That makes the SOIC video's timing notable. Its host argues that the US midterms, where Democrats are leaning anti-data-center and floating moratoria, could puncture the AI trade and send foreign institutional money back to India. He expects Indian AI-export names such as optical fiber and gas-engine makers, which have traded at around 110 times earnings, to re-rate toward 50 to 60 times, since they depend on hyperscaler spending. He also points out that emerging markets have been flat for over a decade, with the Brazilian ETF going nowhere and Africa's 2011 breakout delivering nothing. His claim is that this has made India look like an attractive place to park capital. That is a forecast, not a fact, and it is exactly the type of narrative Dhawan would tell you to treat with caution.

Financially Free's study of quick-service restaurants shows how a story can be tested against numbers. Domino's operator Jubilant was a darling from 2012 to 2020, but KFC's operator Devyani is roughly flat at around 120 rupees after four years, and Pizza Hut-linked names have been the weakest on nearly every metric. The creator's diagnosis: pre-Covid the business was dine-in, now it is delivery, and Domino's old 20-minute delivery advantage disappeared once Zomato and others arrived. Inflation hit costs while sales per store stagnated, so volume must have suffered. Now the numbers are turning. Break-even per store that once took years now takes two to two and a half. Same-store sales growth is positive again for KFC and accelerating, Burger King is recovering, and the stocks are moving above their 200-day averages. He is careful to ask whether this is permanent, not to assume it, and he flags that after the accounting change, rent no longer sits inside EBITDA, so you should check the pre-IndAS number.

What links the three is discipline about evidence. Dhawan buys what is rising and sells what stops. SOIC reads macro events as triggers for rotation but admits he is forecasting. The QSR analyst waits for same-store sales to actually turn. None of them say the story doesn't matter; they say it shouldn't be the reason you act.

For an individual investor, the practical advice is unglamorous: decide your rules before the narrative arrives, size positions so a 30 percent drawdown is survivable, and treat any confident prediction, including the ones above, as input rather than instruction.

briefs.title: Socratic Questioning Is for Finding Out, Not Winning
briefs.body:
A philosophy channel called Unsolicited advice sells Socrates as a debating weapon: its 18-minute explainer is titled "How to Win a Debate Without Even Trying." The packaging undersells the content. What the video actually lays out is a sequence of six kinds of questions, drawn from Plato's dialogues and sharpened with the creator's own additions, that make an argument productive whoever turns out to be right. Below is the method as the video teaches it, followed by our own analysis of where it holds up, where it breaks, and how to use it at work.

## The method, in six questions

First, argue before you argue. Most disagreements that go nowhere are two people using one word to mean two different things. The video's example: if you are a deist (God started the universe and stepped back) and I assume you are a theist (God is still involved in it), my arguments from the problem of evil miss you entirely, and "God exists" and "God doesn't exist" don't even contradict each other. Political labels like "socialist" or "right-wing" fail the same way. So Socrates opens almost every dialogue by asking what a key word such as justice, beauty or love means. The creator adds a second opening question: under what circumstances would you, or I, be wrong? Someone who can't imagine any is probably not worth debating, and the answer shows what actually holds a belief up. A person who supports legal euthanasia but would drop that view if most patients were being pressured into it is telling you they judge laws by their consequences.

Second, play the ignoramus. "I'm not sure I completely understand your position" is one of the most disarming sentences available. It signals you aren't there to humiliate anyone, and it licenses the question that does the real work: what do you mean by that? People change their minds far more readily when they find the hole themselves. In Plato's Republic, Thrasymachus claims justice is whatever serves the stronger; pressed to pin that down, he gets caught between what the powerful want and what actually benefits them, because the powerful can be wrong about their own interests. The modern version: "we shouldn't listen to immoral people" becomes, after two rounds of "what do you mean?", a claim about moral questions only. That is a much smaller claim, and nobody had to say "you're wrong."

Third, separate causes from reasons. "Why do you think that?" hides two questions. What caused the belief? Perhaps hearing suffering patients ask to die, and the emotion that followed. What are the reasons for it? Perhaps a principle that people may do as they wish with their own bodies when no one else is directly harmed. Reasons can be tested with logic; causes often can't, and someone who holds a view because of a father's dying words won't be argued out of it. Asking both questions also blocks the most common shortcut in public argument: inventing the other side's motives ("you just want people to suffer") and arguing with those instead.

Fourth, try on other lives. The creator turns a viral TV-chef put-down ("if my grandmother had wheels, she would have been a bike") into a thought experiment: with wheels instead of legs you would think in distances rather than steps and notice every missing ramp. If you had grown up in a collapsing country, you might rank security above freedom. Asking how your view would look from a different life surfaces options you didn't know you were ignoring. With someone defending the death penalty, it becomes a concrete question: what rate of wrongful convictions would change your mind? The creator says they read cynical philosophers on purpose, to correct for their own optimism.

Fifth, follow the implications. This is the reductio ad absurdum: assume the position is true, see what follows, and if what follows is absurd, the position falls. Formally it is modus tollens: if A then B; not B; therefore not A. The video's example is crude moral relativism. If moral truth is relative to each person, moral disputes could never be resolved; they can be resolved; so relativism fails. Aquinas built much of the Summa Theologica this way, and Socrates does it throughout Plato's dialogues. The questions to ask: if I believed this, what else would follow? And if I didn't, what would follow from that?

Sixth, question the questions. Step back and ask whether you really understand the other view, whether you have mixed up causes and reasons, and what you still haven't asked. The video admits this is less a technique than an attitude, epistemic humility, and that the only way to get better at the other five is practice.

## Our analysis

It helps to know where the framework comes from. The six steps closely track a modern taxonomy of "Socratic questions" associated with the critical-thinking educator Richard Paul: clarification, assumptions, reasons and evidence, viewpoints, implications, and questions about the question. That lineage is a strength, because Paul's version was built for teaching, where the questioner wants the other person to understand. But it is not quite what Socrates did. His elenchus was narrower and harsher: extract a definition, win agreement to a few more premises, then show they contradict the definition. Many of the dialogues end in aporia, a shared puzzlement with no winner. Euthyphro simply leaves in a hurry without an answer.

That makes the "win without trying" framing the weakest part of the package. The method did not win Socrates many arguments in the social sense: Athens tried and executed him in 399 BC, and in Plato's Apology he traces the hostility to his habit of showing prominent men that they knew less than they thought. People can tell a question asked to learn from one asked to trap them, and feigned ignorance used as a tactic reads as condescension. The video's caveat that all of this must come from genuine curiosity isn't a footnote; it is the whole method. Used as a weapon, it produces exactly the defensiveness it was meant to avoid.

The best single question in the video is the creator's own addition, "under what circumstances would you be wrong?", and it has a blind spot. It works on empirical claims: what false-conviction rate, what market data, what test result. Many serious disagreements bottom out in values instead, such as liberty against security or autonomy against the sanctity of life, where no evidence would settle it. Someone who can't name a fact that would change their mind isn't necessarily arguing in bad faith; they may have just shown you that the disagreement is about priorities, not facts. Treat a blank answer as a map, not a verdict, and follow up with: is this about what is true, or about what matters more?

The line between causes and reasons is also blurrier in practice than the video suggests. Research on motivated reasoning, including Jonathan Haidt's social intuitionist model, finds that people often reach a judgment by intuition and build the reasons afterwards to defend it. So asking for reasons can surface a rationalization, and refuting it changes nothing. Jonathan Swift made the point three centuries ago: reasoning will never make a man correct an ill opinion which by reasoning he never acquired. A practical test that combines the first and third questions: "If that reason turned out to be false, would you change your view?" If the answer is no, the reason wasn't load-bearing. Keep looking.

The reductio has a well-known escape hatch, summed up in the philosophers' quip that one person's modus ponens is another's modus tollens. "If A then B; B is absurd; so not A" only works if both sides agree that B is absurd. The relativist in the video's example can simply bite the bullet and deny that moral disputes are ever really resolved. So the fifth question loops back to the first: consequences have no force until you share some premises. The six questions are less a sequence than a cycle.

One addition we would make to the second question comes from the philosopher Daniel Dennett, who adapted it from the game theorist Anatol Rapoport: before you criticize a view, restate it so clearly and fairly that the other person says, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way." It is the clearest proof that "I'm not sure I understand" was sincere, and it often settles half the argument before it starts.

The method pays off most when it is pointed inward and at your own team rather than at opponents. Before buying a stock, write down what would make you sell; that is the first question applied to a thesis. A project pre-mortem, the psychologist Gary Klein's exercise of imagining the plan has already failed and asking why, is the fifth question run backwards. In product reviews, half the arguments about "engagement" or "activation" are disagreements over definitions in disguise. In a hiring debrief, "I liked them" is a cause and "they solved the systems problem cleanly" is a reason, and only one of those belongs in the decision.

A version to keep for your next disagreement: What do we each mean by the key word? What would change my mind, and theirs? Can I state their view so well that they would sign it? Is my reason load-bearing, or a cause in disguise? If I'm right, what else has to be true? And what haven't I asked yet?
